title: Family Caregiver Study Bischofswiesen
summary:
Background:
Parents of infants (0–12 months) and young children (1–6 years) represent a high-risk group for psychosocial stress. For this target group, the specific term parental burnout has been coined. It describes a condition of parental exhaustion, emotional distancing, and strong doubts about one’s own parenting competence. This phenomenon occurs independently of socioeconomic status and can negatively affect the family atmosphere and, consequently, the child.
Furthermore, a nationwide representative study from 2022 found that about 21.5% of all parents reported moderate to clinically significant psychological distress—an increase compared to 15.7% in 2015. In the preceding study from 2015, it was shown that psychosocial stress among parents of children aged 0–3 years had increased. This is particularly concerning since parental stress can affect children’s development. Physicians documented signs of regulatory disorders and developmental delays more frequently in children whose parents reported clinically significant psychological distress. As part of the 2017 hkk Health Report, 733 individuals insured by hkk who had participated in a mother/father-child preventive cure under §24 SGB V in 2015 were contacted. A total of 343 participants completed the questionnaire. Of these, 62% rated their health condition immediately after the measure as “good” to “very good,” but only 20% did so one to two years later. However, a methodological limitation of this study is that the survey asked participants retrospectively about three different points in time, which may have caused response bias.

Caring for a dependent family member can likewise lead to physical and mental health problems such as pain, depression, anxiety, and stress-related disorders. Women, married individuals, and those providing care for more than 20 hours per week or for persons with dementia are particularly at risk. This is critical given that nearly five million people in Germany require care, and about 80% are cared for in private households. More than half of these individuals are looked after exclusively by family members, most of whom are women aged 50–69 years.
The health effects of informal caregiving are explained by adapted stress models. Care-related stressors and insufficient coping strategies can lead to negative emotional, physical, or behavioral reactions. In this context, targeted therapeutic interventions and concepts that strengthen and empower family caregivers are needed.
With the Care Realignment Act (Pflege-Neuausrichtungsgesetz) of 2012, the legal basis for preventive and rehabilitation measures for caregivers was established under §23 SGB V. However, there are currently few studies that scientifically evaluate the effectiveness of these measures.

Research question and methodology:
Under §§24 and 23 of the German Social Code, Book V (SGB V), entitlement to medical preventive measures for mothers/fathers and family caregivers was established. The effectiveness of these measures, however, has so far been scarcely investigated. Therefore, through our online survey, we aim to gain insights into the health effects of these preventive measures. Specifically, we seek to examine whether participation in a medical preventive program can help reduce the occurrence of physical and psychological complaints.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Mothers or fathers and informal caregivers aged 18 years or older who participate in a medical preventive care program pursuant to §24 or §23 of the German Social Code, Book V (SGB V), at the Augustinum Preventive Care Clinic Berchtesgadener Land will be included.
Exclusion criteria:
None.
